categories.name: It works
categories.notes: Build succeeds with 0 errors; the 10 warnings are the scaffold's NU1902/NU1903 ImageSharp advisories, so none were introduced. / returns 200 through the '/' domain on the Blog (blogHome) page and lists both posts as cards with title, excerpt and date, and the links work. Both posts render all their blocks (rich text, image, quote, rich text) with no render errors, and the front-page hero renders. 6 of the provided Unsplash photos are imported into a Blog media folder and served through signed GetCropUrl URLs (3/3 load). All content is published.

categories.name: Content modeling
categories.notes: Folders and kinds are right: blogHome and blogPost are in Pages, the 4 element types (heroBlock, richTextBlock, imageBlock, quoteBlock) are in Blocks, and siteRoot is in Repositories (8/8). The block grid is on both page types with a sensible 4-block set: hero, rich text with heading, image with caption, and quote with attribution (7/7). Structure: siteRoot is the only root type, siteRoot allows blogHome, blogHome allows blogPost, templates are assigned, aliases are camelCase, and 'Blog Block Grid' sits in /Custom/Umbraco.BlockGrid (5/5). Hygiene: excerpt and coverImage are real properties, but there is no publish-date property (the listing and post show UpdateDate as 'Updated ...'). The coverImage property is filled on both posts but rendered nowhere (not on cards, not on posts), and 'title' duplicates the node name (3/5).

categories.name: Code architecture & conventions
categories.notes: blogHome.cshtml and blogPost.cshtml render blocks with Html.GetBlockGridHtmlAsync(Model, "blocks"). There are no custom loops, and the scaffold's blockgrid partials are unchanged. There are 4 exact-alias adapters in Views/Partials/blockgrid/Components that take BlockGridItem<T>, map to plain models and call Component.InvokeAsync with no markup. There are 4 ViewComponents (Hero, RichText, ImageBlock, Quote) with Default.cshtml views typed to plain models in Models/Blocks, with no Umbraco dependencies. Program.cs and appsettings.json are untouched, there are no migrations, and the code uses friendly Children<T>()/Url()/GetCropUrl. Styling uses Tailwind built to wwwroot/dist/site.css. Minor, not deducted: both templates duplicate the full HTML shell and header (no shared layout), and the Hero view hard-codes an 'MCP & Umbraco' eyebrow.

categories.name: Content & presentation
categories.notes: Both posts are on topic and accurate ('Why MCP is Awesome': one protocol for every tool, an open standard; 'MCP and Umbraco': the MCP server wrapping the Management API). But they are thin: each has two short rich text blocks of 2 paragraphs each (about 150 words in total), plus one image and a one-line quote. The quotes carry invented attributions ('Anonymous integration developer', 'The Umbraco editorial team'). The images are relevant and credited in their captions (3/6). The look is clean and coherent: a dark hero with a network photo, a card listing, readable post typography with a max-w-3xl column, and a styled pull quote. However, the cards have no image even though a coverImage exists, the image block's 6-column span is ignored (no grid layout CSS, so it renders full width), and the front page is just a hero plus the list (3/4).

categories.name: Process & honesty
categories.notes: Schema, media, content, domain and publishing were all done over the Umbraco MCP server (67 calls, 38 writes). There was no Management API, database, uSync or migration use. The order was followed: model -> content -> stop/build/restart -> Razor. create-template rejected the Razor content, so empty template records were created over MCP and the views were written to disk afterwards. The model read only files inside the project (its boot logs went to /tmp) (3/3). The final report is accurate: it describes what was built, the URLs and the template workaround, and the warnings it mentions are pre-existing. It calls the image 'half-width', which is how it is configured but not how it renders (2/2).

summary: A clean MCP-built blog: blogHome and blogPost with a 4-block grid (hero, rich text, image, quote), rendered by the book (exact-alias adapters -> ViewComponents -> plain models), with a correct domain, media and publishing, and everything works. Points are lost on thin posts with invented quote attributions, an unused coverImage, and no real publish-date property.
strengths: Textbook rendering pipeline: GetBlockGridHtmlAsync, 4 exact-alias adapters, 4 ViewComponents, plain models in Models/Blocks
Everything built through MCP in the right order, with no out-of-channel shortcuts
Correct folders, element kinds, allowed children, domain and block grid data type location
Provided Unsplash photos imported into a media folder and served through signed GetCropUrl URLs, with credits in captions
